articles.title: CVE-2026-114938: OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Vulnerable To Pre-Authentication RCE (Java4Shell)
articles.context: 2 Critical), a severe heap memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated (intrinsic) Base64 decoder on certain CPUs
articles.full_text: IntroductionOn November 17, 2026, security researchers from Calif.io publicly disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS v4.0: 9.2 Critical), a severe heap memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated (intrinsic) Base64 decoder on certain CPUs. The disclosure coincided with coordinated advisories from the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group and Oracle’s November 17, 2026 security patch release.Because Base64 decoding is foundational to network protocols, this runtime-level vulnerability can be reached in enterprise applications that pass attacker-controlled input to the affected decoder. Calif.io demonstrated pre-authentication Remote Code Execution (RCE) in default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Additionally, post-authentication RCE was achieved in Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Netflix Spinnaker, as well as a client-side TLS exploit affecting Java clients connecting to a malicious server. Immediate patching for affected environments is strongly recommended, alongside other mitigation steps outlined in this advisory. Zscaler’s security team is actively analyzing this issue across both production and corporate environments. We will continue to update the Zscaler Trust post and this advisory as new information becomes available. RecommendationsOrganizations running Java workloads on x86-64 infrastructure should take the following actions:Apply vendor patches immediately: Upgrade OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM, and all downstream OpenJDK distributions to the patched builds released on or after November 17, 2026 (such as Oracle Java SE 17.0.21.1, 8u513, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1 security updates) and restart all running JVM processes and containers.Apply JVM flag workarounds where patching is delayed: If an immediate JDK upgrade is not feasible, defenders can completely disable the vulnerable assembly code path by passing either of the following flags at JVM startup (e.g., via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS):-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics (Recommended): Disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding intrinsics across all architectures, falling back to safe Java bytecode execution.-XX:UseAVX=2 (x86-64 hosts only): Restricts HotSpot to AVX2 instructions, preventing the use of AVX-512 VBMI instructions. Warning: Use this flag only on x86-64 machines; OpenJDK on ARM64 does not recognize this flag and will fail to start.After adjusting startup command lines and parameters, restart all running JVM processes and containers.Check Host CPUs for AVX-512 VBMI Exposure: Because CVE-2026-114938 is hardware-dependent, administrators can determine if the CPU of a Linux system is capable of executing the vulnerable Base64 decoder by inspecting the /proc/cpuinfo file and determining if all four of the following flags are present: avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2. If a system is not susceptible, the JVM patches should still be applied in accordance with local policy and best practices.Eliminate public exposure: Place internet-facing Java applications (such as Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory, and PingFederate) behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Enable reverse-proxy request buffering (Defense-in-Depth): Many remote heap grooming techniques rely on partial HTTP requests to prepare the heap for successful exploitation. Enabling full HTTP request-body buffering at the reverse proxy (e.g., Nginx proxy_request_buffering on;) disrupts multi-connection timing alignment—though note this is not a complete mitigation for single-request chains (such as Elasticsearch) or upgraded WebSocket tunnels. Affected JDK Distributions And VersionsCVE-2026-114938 affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer, as well as specific performance/patch builds across Oracle Java SE and downstream OpenJDK distributions as shown in the table below:Vendor / CategoryAffected Products & VersionsRemediation / PatchOpenJDK (Upstream)OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newerApply OpenJDK 2026-11-17 advisory patches, or if patching is delayed, use -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround.Oracle Java SE / Oracle GraalVM8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3 (and prior unpatched builds with the affected Base64 decoder)Upgrade to the applicable Oracle November 17, 2026 patch (e.g., Java SE 17.0.21.1).Downstream OpenJDK DistributionsAmazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDKUpgrade to a build that fixes CVE-2026-114938, or if patching is delayed, apply -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround.Table 1: Affected JDK distributions and versions.Hardware prerequisitesThe vulnerable assembly routine is only emitted by the HotSpot C2 JIT compiler on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI (avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, bmi2):Vulnerable Intel server CPUs: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite RapidsVulnerable AMD server and desktop CPUs: AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer (e.g., EPYC Genoa / Bergamo / Turin, Ryzen 7000/9000 series)Not affected: ARM64 processors (e.g., AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon, Ampere Altra) and older x86-64 CPUs lacking AVX-512 VBMI. Technical AnalysisHow it worksWhile Java is traditionally regarded as a memory-safe language that abstracts raw pointer arithmetic away from developers, the OpenJDK HotSpot Virtual Machine itself relies heavily on C, C++, and hand-rolled assembly intrinsics to maximize throughput on modern hardware. Specifically, OpenJDK’s C2 Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler includes an optimized x86-64 Base64 decoding routine leveraging AVX-512 VBMI vector instructions. Due to an arithmetic underflow when calculating the store mask for improperly padded Base64 tails, malformed Base64 input can be used to trigger a 62-byte heap out-of-bounds write.Base64 decoding sits at the foundation of many network protocols including HTTP authentication, cookies, authorization tokens, TLS certificate parsing, REST API payloads, and file uploads. Thus, the attack surface for this vulnerability is significant. The figure below shows how malformed input can lead to heap corruption.Figure 1: CVE-2026-114938: Java4Shell Exploit Workflow ConclusionCVE-2026-114938 ("Java4Shell") demonstrates that even memory-safe managed runtimes like Java are susceptible to classic memory corruption when low-level assembly intrinsics miscalculate bounds. Organizations running affected Java builds on x86-64 processors with the required instruction support should patch immediately . Where immediate patching is not possible, restart affected JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to temporarily disable the vulnerable code path. Zscaler CoverageZscaler has deployed the following protections for CVE-2026-114938:Zscaler DeceptionZscaler Deception customers can deploy Private Threat Intelligence decoys for the following applications to detect Java4Shell exploitation attempts and generate high-fidelity alerts:Apache SolrJenkinsAtlassian ConfluenceAtlassian JiraElasticsearchCustomers can configure an orchestration rule to add any IP addresses interacting with these decoys to a firewall block list. How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table outlines typical attack stages for CVE-2026-114938 and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler:Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and prioritize vulnerable Java deployments with Zscaler Exposure Management; eliminate externally exposed internal Java applications by placing them behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Prevent compromiseInspect inbound and outbound traffic with ZPA and Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to detect and block malformed Base64 padding tails, protect Java clients against the client-side TLS exploit vector by routing egress traffic through ZIA with full SSL/TLS inspection.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app and app-to-app microsegmentation for crown-jewel workloads, deploy Zscaler Deception decoys to detect lateral movement.Use Zscaler Microsegmentation to restrict workload-to-workload traffic and limit lateral movement if a Java workload is compromised.Prevent data lossInspect outbound responses and egress traffic across all channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP) to detect and block JavaBleed heap memory leaks containing private keys, credentials, or PII. Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Network-level indicatorsJIT warm-up floods: High volumes of rapid, repetitive requests containing valid Base64 fields targeting endpoints that invoke java.util.Base64.Decoder.Connection parking (remote heap grooming): Multiple concurrent TCP/HTTP connections from the same source IP delivering partial HTTP request bodies, pausing awaiting TCP ACK, and releasing the final bytes simultaneously.Malformed Base64 tail triggers: Base64 strings whose length is a multiple of 64 bytes (64 or 128 characters) immediately followed by an invalid padded tail (=, ==, X=, X==, XY=, ===), such as AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= (64 bytes + =) or 128 × "A" + "=".JavaBleed response anomalies: Abnormally large HTTP responses returned immediately after a spike in IllegalArgumentException errors.Host-level indicatorsSpikes in java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: High rates of IllegalArgumentException: Illegal base64 character or invalid padding exceptions in application logs.JVM crash logs (hs_err_pid*.log): Repeated HotSpot SIGSEGV crashes in G1 GC routines or StubRoutines::base64_decodeBlock.Suspicious JVM child processes: Java process spawning unexpected OS shells or reconnaissance commands.

articles.title: Attackers Exploit Optimizely Flaw To Inject Malicious JavaScript
articles.context: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow
articles.full_text: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow. Optimizely is a platform used to create, manage, test, and personalize digital content and websites. The flaw allowed the attacker to edit the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field. Customers use this field to add custom code that runs on pages that load the Optimizely snippet. By abusing this mechanism, the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The code was then delivered to visitors’ browsers through the Optimizely snippets, including snippets served from Optimizely’s content delivery network (CDN).The attack highlights the continued risk posed by third-party script dependencies and software supply chain compromises, particularly when websites rely on trusted third-party platforms to deliver JavaScript that runs in visitors’ browsers.Optimizely reported that it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code from affected projects, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and notified impacted customers.The malicious payload was designed to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skim payment card details, steal cookies, capture page screenshots, and deliver iOS exploits to iPhones and iPads. Organizations using Optimizely, or similar third-party JavaScript platforms, should treat this incident as a reminder to review third-party script governance, monitoring, and browser-side security controls. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz identified more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script. These findings suggest a broader impact across organizations and industry verticals than previously reported. The affected domains span industries including the following:Airlines and TravelAutomotiveBanking and FinanceE-commerceInsuranceNews and MediaProperty and Real EstateRetail and FashionSmart HomeSportsTechnology and SaaSTelecommunications RecommendationsFor end users who visited affected sitesMonitor bank and credit card statements for suspicious activity.Review cryptocurrency transactions made on or around November 16, 2026.Be cautious of unexpected account activity on sites visited during the incident.Update iOS and iPadOS devices to the latest available security version.Change passwords for accounts used on potentially affected websites, especially if the same credentials are reused elsewhere.For organizations using OptimizelyReview Optimizely project configurationAudit all Project JavaScript fields for unauthorized or unexpected code.Review recent changes, user activity, account creation events, and administrative access.Confirm whether any project snippets were modified during the exposure window.Verify that production pages load only approved versions of Optimizely snippets.Rotate and reset accessReset credentials for affected Optimizely administrative users.Rotate API tokens, session tokens, and integration keys associated with Optimizely.Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users with access to experimentation or web personalization platforms.Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) in enforcement mode where possibleRestrict script execution to approved domains.Limit where pages can send requests and load images and frames using connect-src, img-src, frame-src, and related CSP directives.Use CSP reporting to identify unexpected browser-side activity.Reduce third-party JavaScript riskMaintain an inventory of third-party scripts loaded across websites.Review whether each third-party script is still required.Apply least-privilege principles to third-party tags and tag management platforms.Monitor third-party script changes and unexpected behavior. How It WorksOptimizely Web Experimentation allows site owners to run A/B tests, personalization logic, and other front-end experiments by loading JavaScript on customer websites. The Project JavaScript field is designed to let customers add custom JavaScript that executes on any page that loads the Optimizely snippet.Public reporting indicates that the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into the Project JavaScript field of affected customer projects. The injected code was then delivered through legitimate Optimizely snippets. As a result, when visitors loaded a page with a modified snippet, the injected JavaScript could run in their browsers.Scope of script activity: The observed JavaScript activity is primarily limited to the browser context of the website where the scripts are loaded. The wallet replacement, clipboard manipulation, form monitoring, card-skimming, screen capture, and network-hooking behaviors operate inside the current page, its accessible DOM, same-origin frames, page-initiated requests, and JavaScript-accessible cookies or browser APIs. By design, this JavaScript cannot directly inspect other browser tabs, unrelated websites, other sites’ cookies, local files, or global browser activity. The main exception is the iOS/iPadOS exploit-delivery branch: if one of the delivered exploit chains succeeds, the resulting impact could potentially exceed normal web-page sandbox restrictions.Attack chainThe figure below shows how malicious JavaScript reached website visitors through Optimizely snippets.Figure 1: Attack chain showing how a threat actor injected malicious JavaScript into Optimizely customer projects.Initial access and injectionAs stated above, the attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation account signup flow. This flaw allowed unauthorized write access to the Project JavaScript field for multiple customer projects. Modified snippets were served through existing delivery paths, including Optimizely’s CDN (including cdn.optimizely.com) and, in some cases, customer domains. This made the attack more effective because many affected websites already trusted and allowed Optimizely scripts.Malicious JavaScript payloadIn most affected snippets, the injected code acted as a loader that fetched a second-stage JavaScript payload named track.js from attacker-controlled infrastructure such as 1688360[.]cc. The JavaScript payload provided the main malicious functionality, and ran in the visitor’s browser within the context of the affected website.The following flowchart shows what track.js does after it runs in a visitor’s browser. Figure 2: Clipboard hijacking, card skimming, cookie theft, screen capturing, and attempted exploit delivery on iOS and iPadOS.Cryptocurrency address replacement The script monitors page content, clipboard operations, and network-transmitted data for cryptocurrency wallet addresses. Targeted cryptocurrencies include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, Litecoin, Toncoin, Bitcoin Cash, and Dogecoin. When the script detects a valid wallet address, the script attempts to replace it with an attacker-controlled wallet address. Cookie theft and screen capture Cookie theft and screen capture happens only when a valid crypto wallet address is replaced and the element is visible. In that case, the JavaScript payload script loaded the legitimate html2canvas.min.js to capture a screenshot of the page, along with the page URL, cookies, original wallet address, and other metadata. This data is sent to the attacker endpoint https://1688360[.]cc/hit.php, likely so the operator can validate successful replacement activity and capture the victim’s session context. The JavaScript payload could collect browser cookies from the affected website, with some exceptions such as if the HttpOnly flag was set. This could cause users to unknowingly send cryptocurrency to the attacker instead of the intended recipient.Payment card skimmingLater versions of the payload added payment card skimming functionality. The script monitors input and textarea elements, keyboard events, form submissions, and web requests for payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV values on the compromised website. Captured card data was to an attacker-controlled endpoint (1688360[.]cc/card.php). Note the skimmer could not read payment details entered inside secure cross-origin payment iframes, such as hosted payment fields from providers like Stripe or Adyen.Attempted iOS exploit delivery For visitors using iPhones or iPads, the malware reportedly attempted to load the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits. The payload used device and browser checks to decide whether to attempt iOS-specific exploitation. When the payload identified a visitor’s device as an iPhone or iPad, it added two script elements to the page to load external JavaScript files. Indicators of these pages are the elements data-channel-code, data-chain-url, and data-cfasync attributes.The script injected a hidden iframe in some cases (hxxps://eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/JIUJIU888/weifile[.]html) on devices it identified as running iOS 18.6 or earlier. The iframe is positioned off-screen with zero width and height, suggesting it is not intended to be visible to the user. iOS exploit delivery componentstrack.js is the browser-side payload. It checks for iOS or iPadOS and loads additional components when it detects either operating system.boot.js is the main iOS loader. It uses Safari and iOS version information to select the next delivery path.weifile.html provides a separate delivery path for selected iOS and iPadOS versions. It loads index.js.index.js initializes an obfuscated loader, decodes embedded modules, reports device and domain metadata, and may fetch additional modules (if required). The following table summarizes the two modules embedded in index.js.Embedded Module IdentifierDescription57620206d62079baad0e57e6d9ec93120c0f5247Utility/runtime helper module providing encoding, binary parsing, numeric conversion, URL normalization, and typed-array/DataView helpers.14669ca3b1519ba2a8f40be287f646d4d7593eb0Browser environment profiling and anti-analysis module that checks runtime capabilities, storage behavior, WebRTC, MathML rendering, WebAssembly behavior, and automation indicators such as navigator.webdriver.Table 1: Functions of the two modules embedded in index.js. ConclusionThe Optimizely incident highlights how attackers can compromise trusted third-party JavaScript supply chains to reach users across many websites at once. By abusing a legitimate experimentation feature, the attacker delivered injected JavaScript through snippets that affected websites already trusted. Note the malicious JavaScript code can run in visitors’ browsers without any obvious change to the page. The card-skimming and wallet-replacement behavior should be understood as page-context activity, not browser-wide monitoring. These scripts act within the compromised site where they are loaded. Broader impact would depend on successful exploitation by the iOS/WebKit exploit chain. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler ThreatLabz team has deployed protections for the indicators of compromise associated with this campaign.Zscaler Advanced Threat ProtectionHTML.Malurl.OPZHTML.Phish.Gen.LVHTML.Malurl.Gentp.LZHTML.Phish.Gen.Rc.A.ENHTML.Malurl.Gen.LZJS.PWS.Optimizely How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows Zscaler’s recommended mitigations by attack stage.Attack StageRecommended MitigationPrevent compromiseEnable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Use Advanced Threat Protection to detect malicious scripts. Configure policies to block Newly Registered and Observed Domains.Route server egress through Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to detect and block post-compromise activity.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall to extend controls across all ports/protocols.Use Zscaler Zero Trust Browser to isolate high-risk browsing sessions and reduce endpoint exposure to malicious web content.Prevent lateral threat movementUse Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) to enforce least-privilege user-to-application segmentation.Use Zscaler Deception to detect attacker movement after initial compromise. Monitor for suspicious access to internal applications following web application crashes or abnormal behavior.Detect post-exploitation activityUse Zscaler Managed Detection & Response (MDR) and Threat Hunting to investigate suspicious process behavior, command execution, unusual outbound connections, container runtime anomalies, and web application worker crashes.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP).Monitor for unusual uploads, archive transfers, credential exposure, or data movement following suspected exploitation. articles.title: CVE-2026-111497: Node2Shell / HTTP2Shell Vulnerability May Allow RCE
articles.context: ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below
articles.full_text: IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, the Node.js project disclosed CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Google’s Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. The vulnerability is also known as Node2Shell and more recently as HTTP2Shell. The CVE score, filed by Google as the numbering authority, is 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. The flaw can be triggered when a vulnerable process decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. Successful exploitation may result in process crashes, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution (RCE). Imperva reported demonstrating code execution in fresh containers running the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with multiple attempts required in its test environment. The vulnerable Brotli decoder may be present in a range of runtimes, libraries, and software packages, including Node.js, Bun, Python Brotli bindings, .NET, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Java brotli4j, libbrotli, curl/libcurl through Brotli dependencies, and Linux distribution packages. Applications may be exposed if they decompress attacker-controlled data using a vulnerable decoder. The vulnerability may be reachable through both inbound and outbound traffic paths. A malicious client could send a crafted request with Content-Encoding: br to a vulnerable server-side component that performs Brotli request decompression. Conversely, a malicious or compromised server could return a crafted Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable client application that automatically decodes Brotli responses. ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below. RecommendationsZscaler recommends the following measures to address CVE-2026-111497 and monitor for potentially related activity:Patch vulnerable runtimes and libraries. Upgrade vulnerable runtimes, packages, and infrastructure components to the patched versions listed in the Vulnerable Versions table. Prioritize services that decompress untrusted Brotli data, including internet-facing applications that accept compressed request bodies and services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs. Validate each vulnerable component independently. Updating the system-wide libbrotli package may not remediate applications that statically bundle Brotli or ship their own decoder copy.Rebuild and redeploy containers. Use patched base images, runtimes, and libraries, and verify the versions in running workloads. Updating a host’s libraries does not update copies bundled within container images.Disable Brotli decoding where patching is delayed. If immediate patching is not possible, disable Brotli decompression on vulnerable paths where supported, following vendor guidance and testing for application compatibility.Monitor for exploitation and post-exploitation behavior. Investigate the following: Unexpected process crashes in Node.js, Bun, Python, .NET, Envoy Proxy, or service mesh workloads.Repeated malformed Brotli payloads.Requests containing Content-Encoding: br to endpoints that normally do not receive compressed request bodies.Abnormal memory access violations or segmentation faults.Web server or application worker crashes after compressed request handling.Unexpected child processes spawned by web application runtimes.Unexpected outbound connections following crashes or the processing of malformed compressed input. Vulnerable VersionsThe following table lists vulnerable versions and corresponding fixes for selected software that incorporates the Brotli decoder. ProductVulnerable VersionsPatched VersionsGoogle Brotli1.0.3 < 1.0.10 (semver)1.0.10Google Brotli1.1.0 < 1.1.1 (semver)1.1.1Google Brotli1.2.0 < 1.2.1 (semver)1.2.1Node.js22.0.0 - 22.23.322.23.4Node.js24.0.0 - 24.22.024.22.1Node.js26.0.0 - 26.12.026.12.1Bun< 1.4.41.4.4.NET8.0.0 - 8.0.328.0.33.NET9.0.0 - 9.0.219.0.22.NET10.0.0 - 10.0.1310.0.14.NET11.0.0-preview.1 - 11.0.0-rc.211.0.0-rc.3.26522.148Python Brotli (PyPI)1.2.01.2.1Python brotlicffi (PyPI)1.2.0.0 - 1.2.0.21.2.1.0Envoy Proxy1.39.2, 1.38.5, 1.37.7, 1.36.111.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, 1.37.8, 1.36.12Java brotli4j< 1.24.01.24.0libbrotli (Debian)1.1.0-21.1.0-2+deb13u1libbrotliVaries by distributionApply vendor security updatesTable 1: Software versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 and the corresponding patched versions. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving CVE-2026-111497 through Zscaler Deception. Within the first 24 hours following public disclosure, Zscaler Deception’s global decoy mesh observed activity from 20 source IP addresses targeting 12 customers across 402 events. Of these events, 40% involved reconnaissance and 60% involved exploitation attempts. How It WorksBrotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It is used for HTTP compression to reduce the size of web content such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and API responses. Brotli-encoded HTTP content is identified by the Content-Encoding: br header.Applications may use Brotli directly or through dependencies such as runtimes, frameworks, HTTP clients, and middleware. In some configurations, these components automatically decompress Brotli-encoded content without application code explicitly calling Brotli APIs.Vulnerability detailsThe flaw occurs in Brotli’s block-decoding logic. When a stream changes block type, the decoder determines the next block type and length. In vulnerable versions, there is a macro (in the fast-path logic) that does not properly check the return value of the DecodeBlockTypeAndLength function, which can cause the decoder to continue processing an invalid state (e.g., when provided a maliciously crafted Brotli stream). This can lead to an out-of-bounds write and be used as a primitive for RCE. The upstream fix modifies the decoder so malformed block-switch conditions return a distinct error that is propagated to the caller, stopping further decoding of the malicious Brotli stream.Attack chainExploitation of CVE-2026-111497 may follow either an inbound or outbound path, depending on where Brotli decompression occurs, as shown in the figure below. Inbound attempts use crafted Brotli-compressed HTTP request bodies while outbound attempts use crafted responses returned by an attacker-controlled or compromised server. These responses may be consumed through fetch(), webhook delivery, URL previews, crawlers or scrapers, and API integrations. In either path, exploitation requires attacker-controlled Brotli data to reach a vulnerable decoder, with compressed HTTP content marked by Content-Encoding: br. Figure 1: Potential inbound and outbound exploitation paths for CVE-2026-111497. ConclusionCVE-2026-111497 affects the Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. Exposure depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled Brotli data to a vulnerable decoder. Organizations should identify vulnerable components and apply corresponding vendor updates, including updates for applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli.Zscaler Deception has observed active reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving this vulnerability.
